idiom_name: ActiveModel::Validations - valid? invoked on demand, errors as the accumulator
implementation_notes: Ruby separates assignment from judgement: including ActiveModel::Validations gives the object a validates DSL, but nothing runs until someone calls valid? (ActiveRecord's save does it for you), and errors is the collection inspected afterwards - that is exactly the deferred gate plus the violation accumulator. Contexts make the check match the action: validate :rule, on: :publish defines a check set that only the publishing path runs, mirroring validateForSave plus validateForPublication, and valid?(:publish) selects it. Memoising by hand (@errors ||= validate!) is the framework-free alternative and is still justified when the rules must stay plain methods rather than DSL declarations.
code_sketch:
class OrderDraft
  include ActiveModel::Validations
  attr_accessor :rows

  validate :rows_present, on: :publish          # runs only for this action

  def rows_present
    errors.add(:rows, "must not be empty") if rows.to_a.empty?
  end
end

draft.valid?(:publish) or abort(draft.errors.full_messages.join(", "))
Repo.save(draft)                                # after the gate
pitfalls: valid? caches nothing: errors are cleared and rebuilt on every call, so a rule with a side effect such as a uniqueness query runs again on each invocation of the gate.
ActiveRecord runs valid? inside save, so a 'deferred' domain gate that actually relies on save-time validation is not deferred at all, and save(validate: false) silently removes the only gate.
Validation contexts drift: a rule declared with on: :publish is invisible to a plain valid?, so a caller that forgets the context sees a valid object whose publish rules never ran.
